segments.title: Sōya and Japan's Antarctic research
segments.summary: The trip closes beside Sōya, the vessel that supported Japan's Antarctic research for many years.
segments.body: Sōya supported Japan's cold-weather Antarctic research for many years. The ship and the Tokyo waterfront provide the setting for this short farewell rather than a technical account of her design or service. The opening seconds link the trip's final reflection to Japan's maritime and scientific history. They also show the Tokyo view remembered from the start of the visit.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke identifies Sōya and describes her long role in Japanese Antarctic research.

segments.title: What field visits contribute to Japanese naval history
segments.summary: The ShipShape visit did not settle every question about Japan's naval past, but it clarified what the group needed to study next.
segments.body: The visit improved the group's historical questions rather than supplying final answers about Japan or its naval history. Work undertaken in Japan gave the crew a clearer sense of the subjects it needed to study. A short trip can expose gaps and redirect later inquiry without resolving the subject. This passage gives the first clear explanation of what the ShipShape visit accomplished.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke says the trip did not answer every question about Japan or its naval history but clarified what the group needed to ask next.

segments.title: How national perspective shapes historical questions
segments.summary: Visiting Japan offered a view of how the country perceives its own history, which helped the group frame better questions for future research.
segments.body: A visit can show how a nation understands its own past, and that perspective affects how historians structure their questions. The twenty-four-day trip could not provide complete answers about Japan or its naval history. It clarified which questions should come next and how they might lead to better answers. This passage gives the video's clearest statement of the historical method behind the ShipShape project.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke says visits reveal how a nation perceives its history and help researchers structure better questions, while twenty-four days cannot supply the answers.
